reading.body:
DFW17 publishes 100,000 square feet of technical space but no IT load figure, leaving its compute capacity unquantified against Texas's 389 MW of published data center capacity across 13 facilities.

The floor area establishes that this is a substantial, purpose-built facility rather than a small edge node. Any translation of square footage into rack count or accelerator count would require assumptions about power density and a power figure that the operator has not disclosed. The compute ceiling relative to AI workloads therefore remains unknown from published data alone.

The four certifications define what workloads the facility can legally host. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment-card data. ISO 27001 certifies the information security management system, a requirement common among enterprise and government AI tenants with data-governance obligations. ISO 9001 certifies the operator's quality management processes. LEED certifies energy and environmental performance. None of these certifications measure AI training density or high-performance compute readiness.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities. Of these, only 13 publish megawatt figures. DFW17 is not among them, so it cannot be ranked within the state's published capacity and does not contribute to the 389 MW total from disclosed facilities. The Dallas-Fort Worth metro concentrates a large share of Texas data center capacity, but how much DFW17 represents of that concentration or the state total is not determinable from public specifications.
